en: #Indian || Now begins the Kenopaniṣad.
Oṃ! May my limbs, speech, breath, sight, hearing, as well as strength and all my senses, flourish;
may everything be grounded in the Upanishads of Brahman.
May I not reject Brahman; may Brahman not reject me; may there be non-rejection, may there be non-rejection for me.
For one who is devoted to that within the self...
May those dharmas found in the Upaniṣads abide in me; may they abide in me.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.
## Part II ## Āūṃ! By whom impelled does the mind fly forth when sent? By whom is the first vital breath joined and set in motion?
By whom impelled do they utter this speech? And what god yokes the eye and the ear? (1)
That which is the hearing of the ear, the mind of the mind, the speech of speech, and the breath of the breath—
that is the eye of the eye. Having transcended these, the wise [attain liberation].
Having departed from this world, they become immortal. || 2 ||
Neither the eye goes there, nor speech, nor the mind;
we do not know, nor do we understand, how one might instruct this.
"That is indeed other than the known, and moreover, above the unknown"—thus have we heard from those of old who explained it to us. || 4 ||
That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed—
know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here.
That which the mind does not perceive, that by which they say the mind is perceived— know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship.
That which one does not see with the eye, that by which the eyes are seen—
know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship.
That which one does not hear with the ear, by which this very ear is heard— that alone know thou to be Brahman, and not that which people here worship as an object.
That by which one breathes through the vital breath (prāṇa), and by which the vital breath itself is led forth—
that alone you should know as Brahman, and not this which people here worship.
Thus ends the first section of the Kenopaniṣad.
If you think, "I know it well," then surely you know only a small portion of the form of Brahman.
Whatever you know of this [sacrifice] and whatever it is among the gods—now, indeed, I consider that very thing to be what must be investigated by you. || 1 ||
"I do not think that one knows well; nor does one know that one does not know.
He among us who knows that, he knows it; and he also knows that one does not know. (2)
That which is not thought is thought by him; he who thinks it does not know it.
It is unknown to those who understand, and known to those who do not understand.
That which is known through awakening is considered [the truth], for through it one finds immortality;
through the Self one finds vigor, and through knowledge one finds immortality.
If one has known [the Self] here, then there is truth; if one has not known it here, there is great ruin.
Having searched among all beings, the wise [attain it].
Having departed from this world, they become immortal. || 5 ||
Thus ends the second section in the Kenopaniṣad.
**Part III** Brahman indeed conquered for the gods; in that victory of Brahman, the gods exulted. || 1 ||

They thought, "This victory is ours alone; this greatness is ours alone. He knew of their [thought], and he manifested himself to them. But they did not recognize him, wondering, "What kind of spirit (yakṣa) is this? || 2 ||
They said to Agni Jātavedas, "Find out what this spirit (yakṣa) is. "So be it," he replied.
He ran toward him; he addressed him, saying, "Who are you? He replied, "I am indeed Agni," or "I am indeed Jātavedas. || 4 ||
"What power do you have against me? he asked; "I could burn all this that is upon the earth," [he replied]. || 5 ||
He placed a blade of grass before him, saying, "Burn this!
It approached with all its speed, but it was unable to burn it; it turned back from that very spot, [the god] thinking, "I am not able to discern what this Yakṣa is. || 6 ||
Then they said to Vāyu, "O Vāyu, find out what this yakṣa is. He replied, "So be it."
He ran toward him; he addressed him, saying, "Who are you? He replied, "I am Vāyu," or rather, "I am Mātariśvan. || 8 ||
"What power do you possess? I shall take all this that exists upon the earth. (9)

He placed a blade of grass before him, saying, "Take this. He went toward it with all his speed, but he was not able to eat it; he turned back from that very spot, saying, "I was not able to discern what this Yakṣa is. || 10 ||
Then they said to Indra, "O Maghavan, find out what this yakṣa is. "So be it," he replied, and he ran toward it; then it vanished from him. || 11 ||
In that very space, he beheld a woman approaching, most beautiful, Umā Haimavatī; he said to her, "What is this yakṣa? || 12 ||
Thus ends the third section in the Kenopaniṣad.
"‘That is Brahman,’ he said. ‘It is indeed in the victory of Brahman that you rejoice.
Then, at that very moment, he understood: ‘This is Brahman. || 1 ||

Therefore, these gods—namely Agni, Vāyu, and Indra—are, as it were, superior to the other gods; for they touched this [Brahman] most closely, and they were the first to recognize it as "Brahman. || 2 ||
Therefore, indeed, Indra surpasses all other gods, for he touched this [Brahman] most closely; for he was the first to know it as "Brahman. || 3 ||
This is its instruction: "When lightning flashes, *ā3*!"; and "when it closes its eyes, *ā3*!"—this is with respect to the divine. || 4 ||
Now, with regard to the internal self, that which moves as it were—the mind—and by means of this, one repeatedly recollects it; this is volition (saṅkalpa). 5.
Therefore, that [Self] should be venerated as "The Forest" (Vana), as "The Forest. He who knows this thus—toward him all beings indeed desire to go.
"Sir, tell me the Upanishad. "The Upanishad has been told to you," he said. "But what is that Upanishad?
"Verily, we have told you the Upanishad concerning Brahman. || 7 ||
For him, austerity, self-restraint, and ritual action are the foundation; the Vedas are all the limbs, and truth is the abode. || 8 ||
Whoever knows this thus, having struck away evil, becomes established in the infinite, highest heavenly world—yes, he becomes established. 9.
Thus ends the fourth section in the Kenopaniṣad.
Oṃ! May my limbs, speech, breath, sight, hearing, and likewise strength and all my senses, increase;
may everything be the Upanishadic Brahman.
May I not reject Brahman; may Brahman not reject me; let there be no rejection, let there be non-rejection for me.
For one who is devoted to that within the self...
May those dharmas found in the Upanishads abide in me; may they abide in me.
Om. Peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the Kenopaniṣad.
